valuing them hundreds of thousands of millions of times more than their own body or all their possessions— who always delights in hearing well-spoken Dharma without weariness or satiety,
whose pure faith is profound, whose nature is gentle, and whose mind and views are upright, loving and respecting [the teacher].
Out of virtue and out of love and reverence for the Dharma, one approaches the Dharma teacher without a mind of challenge or dispute,
with a mind of respect and without arrogance, solely for the purpose of seeking the good rather than to display one's own merit,
desiring to establish the roots of goodness in oneself and others, not for the sake of gain or honor, and with a mind free from defilement, remaining far removed [from such things].
Free from arrogance, free from contempt, and free from timidity; listening at the proper time, listening with earnestness, and listening with reverence;
not for the sake of refutation, not for the sake of conformity, and not seeking out faults;
but with a mind seeking awakening and understanding, with a one-pointed mind, lending an ear to the sound and purifying and collecting [the senses].
Maintain [the practice] and listen to the sublime Dharma.
Regarding the Dharma thus heard, one should form four kinds of perceptions;
the first is the perception of it as a wondrous jewel:
Because it is difficult to obtain.
Second is the perception of it as excellent medicine,
because of its meaning of curing disease.
Third, the perception of it as wealth:
because its meaning is not dissipated.
Fourth, the perception of it as nirvāṇa:
Because it has the meaning of extinguishing suffering,
one conceives of the Dharma as a sublime jewel, since it is the cause for the adornment of the marks and signs [of a Buddha].
Because it is the cause for extinguishing afflictions, one conceives of the Dharma as excellent medicine.
"Because the Dharma is the cause of supernormal powers (abhijñā), one should regard it as being like wealth.
Because the Dharma is the correct and inexhaustible cause, one should regard it as being like nirvāṇa.
Next, the intention for seeking to hear the Dharma is explained.

When seeking inner science (*adhyātma-vidyā*), it is for the sake of practicing the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma through correct cultivation, and for the sake of extensively elucidating it to benefit and awaken others.

When seeking logic (*hetu-vidyā*), it is because one wishes to understand, as they truly are, the faulty arguments in the treatises on causality composed by non-Buddhists; it is because one wishes to subdue the various heterodox disputants so that those who lack pure faith in the True Teaching may gain it, and those who already possess pure faith may cause it to increase and expand further.

When seeking the science of grammar (*śabdavidyā*), it is for the purpose of causing sentient beings who take pleasure in the classical language to develop deep reverence and faith toward the body of the Bodhisattva, and for the purpose of awakening them to enter into the phonetics and etymological explanations of words.
When seeking the science of medicine (*cikitsā-vidyā*), it is for the sake of pacifying the various diseases of sentient beings and for the desire to benefit the entire multitude.

When seeking the science of arts and crafts (*śilpa-karma-sthāna-vidyā*), it is for the purpose of accumulating abundant wealth with little effort, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, to inspire in them a sense of profound wonder, and by means of skillful wisdom to equally distribute benefits, thereby aiding and gathering in immeasurable sentient beings.
How is it taught? For what purpose is it taught?
That which is rightly to be sought is precisely that which is taught; for this purpose it is sought, and for this purpose it is taught.
This intention is for the sake of seeking the welfare of oneself and others; it is taught so as to cause sentient beings to practice the welfare of themselves and others.
The present statement, "What is wholesome and what is unwholesome? asks about the dharmas that are sought.
What is right practice? This refers to the ritual procedures for listening to the Dharma and so forth.
Furthermore, he asks what constitutes pure conduct; this refers to that which is sought.
The Sūtra states: "When the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, and their assemblies of disciples see him asking such questions, they reflect as follows:"
The commentary states:
"Virtuous friends constitute reflection.
The Sūtra says: "O son of good family, O daughter of good family!"
"Seeking purity and wishing to hear the true Dharma," [the Buddha] then preached for him, causing him to attain awakening. Commentary:

To explain correctly is the activity of a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*): to cause those who have not yet understood to awaken, and to cause those who have already understood to know it extensively is "opening.
As the Sūtra says: "Having heard it, they maintain it with right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*)."
The commentary states:
This is the third power of attention (*manasikāra*).
One gives rise to appropriate attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*) and maintains it through right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) without abandoning it.
Sūtra: “By generating the resolve and practicing, one attains the power of diligence, eliminates the obstacle of indolence, and extinguishes all sins.
Commentary: This is the fourth power, the power of the provisions (*saṃbhāra*).
Thus, the myriad practices cultivated over three great eons constitute the provisions for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*).

That the first of the five stages is called the "provisions" stage is an instance of a specific term receiving a general designation, just as in the case of the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) and so forth.
Because one has newly resolved the mind to seek enlightenment (*bodhi*), it receives the name "provisions" (*sambhāra*).
The others receive distinct names because they possess superior, specific practices.
Within this power of the provisions, there are two divisions:
Before the first stage (*bhūmi*) and after the stages;
this refers to the former.
There are four [stages] prior to the stages:
First, the cultivation of the initial resolve; second, the attainment of superior power; third, the removal of hindrances; and fourth, the extinction of transgressions.

One cultivates through the generation of the resolve during the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Therefore, the beginning of the ten stages is called the "Stage of Generating the Resolve" (*cittotpāda-vihāra*), because it is the first emergence of the unsurpassed bodhicitta.
Although [the aspiration] had been generated previously, it had not yet entered the *saṃghāṭī* (the stage of the multitude);
because this marks the initial entry into the *saṃghāṭī*, it receives the name "generated" (*utpāda*).

There are various types of generating the mind: the generation of the mind at the stage of the lineage (*gotra*) characterized by the desire for wholesome dharmas; the generation of the mind through resolute conduct (*adhimukti-caryā*) within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*); and once one has entered the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), it is called the generation of the mind through realization (*adhigama-utpāda*).

Now, through this resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), one gains the mind and the power of diligence (*vīrya-bala*); this is the foremost stage of patience (*kṣānti*). Having attained the five powers (*pañca-balāni*), faith serves as the basis for exertion, yet it does not yet constitute the actual subduing of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Diligence can subdue the afflictions; therefore, it is spoken of here.

Regarding "removing the obstacle of indolence," this refers to the obstacle that is diametrically opposed to the practice of vigor. In reality, all two types of obstacles are simultaneously subdued in this stage; this removes the cause of suffering.
The "extinction of all karmic offenses" refers to the fruit of suffering.

Upon reaching the stage of superior patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) and the stage immediately preceding the first dhyāna (*laukikāgra-dharma*), the fruits of suffering of all evil destinies and the eight difficult conditions (*aṣṭāv akṣaṇāḥ*) will never again arise.

The frequent teaching that the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is free from these two is based on the cessation of their seeds; this [present discussion], however, is based on the stage of suppression (*vibhava-avasthā*) and the attainment of certainty.
Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Although the path of seeing arises, it also abandons the various karmas, fruits, and so forth of the miserable destinies."
For now, let us speak of that which can give rise to afflictions, as it is the root.
It is further stated: "The delusion regarding the defilements of the two evil destinies refers precisely to the various karmas and fruits of those evil destinies."
Sūtra: “Regarding the various points of training (śikṣāpada), by abandoning disrespect and calming the mind of agitation and regret, one enters the first stage (bhūmi).
Commentary: This clarifies the entry into the stages beyond the world (bhūmi).
The ten stages (bhūmis) constitute ten [sections], each containing two parts:
first, the removal of obstacles; second, the attainment of the stage.
Because one attains the four kinds of verified confidence (avaivartika-prasāda) in the first stage, one becomes free from disrespect regarding the points of training (śikṣāpada).
The training rules (*śikṣāpada*) are precisely the precepts; alternatively, all that should be cultivated is termed "training rules.

Their essence is not separate from the Three Jewels, for through pure morality one attains verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*). Thus, one is free from a lack of respect and has forever severed conceptual discrimination.
The mind of agitation and regret is the obstacle of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*).

Although the obstacle of the nature of an ordinary being fully encompasses all obstacles of conceptualization (*vikalpa*), because the obstacle of agitation and regret particularly increases the hindrance to meditative concentration (*samādhi*), this [obstacle] causes one to cultivate concentration, and through concentration, wisdom is generated.

Because this concentration and wisdom are combined, they constitute the Dharma-body; therefore, it is specifically said that [wisdom] eliminates [afflictions], though in principle, this applies to all other aspects as well.
Furthermore, both "preparatory abandonment" (*prahāṇa*) and "actual abandonment" (*samyak-prahāṇa*) receive the name of "abandonment."
The stage of the preparatory severance (*prayoga-prahāṇa*) is long and precedes it;
the stage of actual severance (*maula-prahāṇa*) is brief, being the very moment of entering the mind of the ground.

Since this [text] mostly explains the severance of hindrances based on the former stage, it first speaks of calming the mind of agitation and regret, and subsequently describes the entry into the first ground.
The rest should be understood accordingly.
The Sūtra states: "Relying on the mind of the first bhūmi, one removes the obstacles to benefiting sentient beings and attains entry into the second bhūmi.
The Commentary says:

By means of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) in the second stage, there are three distinctions within the perfection of ethical discipline; therein, the bodhisattva practice for the benefit of sentient beings is preeminent.

At the final moment of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), as one is about to enter the second stage, the power of ethical discipline (*śīla*) increases; because one is about to be able to sever that which is currently manifesting, one is able to bring abundant benefit to living beings.
This is said to remove the obstacle to benefiting others, namely the obstacle of wrong conduct (*mithyāpratipatti-āvaraṇa*); having subdued this obstacle, one attains entry into the second stage.
The Sūtra states: "In this stage, having removed the obstacle of non-affliction, one enters the third stage.
The Commentary says:
This refers precisely to the obstacle of dullness.

In works such as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, that which obstructs the superior wisdom derived from hearing and reflection regarding the dhāraṇīs is termed "obscuration of dullness"; here, however, that which obstructs patience (*kṣānti*) is termed "obscuration of affliction.

Alternatively, the former refers to the root obstruction, which is ignorance (*moha*), and is thus called the "obscuration of dullness," while this refers to its derivative manifestations, namely hatred (*dveṣa*) and so forth, and is thus called the "obscuration of affliction."
Alternatively, by means of the three types of patience: being unable to endure suffering due to the attachment to pleasure and so forth is the affliction of greed;
being unable to endure seeing others inflict harm is the affliction of hatred;
and being unable to accept and endure the two truths upon hearing them is the affliction of delusion.
Upon entering the third stage, one attains these three types of patience; therefore, the obstacle of affliction is eliminated.
The Sūtra states: "In this stage, one eliminates the obstacle to the pliancy and purity of mind, and enters the fourth stage."
The commentary states:

"Purity of mind" refers to the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*). "Mildness" refers to the obstacle of the manifestation of subtle afflictions; that is, these subtle afflictions are the obstacles to this purity.
Alternatively, because these afflictions rely upon the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), they are named after their primary locus as "obstructions to the pliancy and purity of the mind.
As the Sūtra states: "In this stage, one removes the obstructions to skillful means and enters the fifth stage."
The commentary states:

The path of non-differentiation cultivated at this stage is precisely the non-conceptual wisdom that can realize non-differentiated suchness; therefore, one attains the non-distinction between the ultimate and the conventional truths.
Because there is no distinction between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, the subsequently attained wisdom (pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna) cultivates great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Prajñā does not abide in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa; this is termed "skillful means" (*upāya*).

The essence of the fundamental body of the skillful means for nirvāṇa is non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), while its arising function is compassion and wisdom. That which can obstruct this is the obstacle of the Lesser Vehicle’s parinirvāṇa.
Nirvana itself is not an obstacle; rather, it is the mind that feels aversion toward saṃsāra and seeks delight in nirvana that constitutes the obstacle.
This obstacle impedes these skillful means; now, by removing this obstacle, one enters the fifth stage.
Sūtra: "In this stage, one eliminates the obstacles regarding the vision of the ultimate and the conventional, and enters the sixth stage.
Commentary: Regarding what is called the ultimate and the conventional, as is commonly distinguished, each has four types.

Among the various treatises, because they rely on general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), it is said that one practices the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths during the first five stages (*pañca-bhūmi*).

However, one is able to contemplate by unifying the two—the ultimate (*paramārtha*) and the conventional (*saṃvṛti*)—thereby removing the obstacles of their mutual contradiction; otherwise, one cannot achieve the unified contemplation of the ultimate and the conventional.

Because one practices the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths, one is still unable to eliminate the two marks of defilement and purity, for these two marks arise based on the ultimate (paramārtha) and the conventional (saṃvṛti).

Now, from the perspective of their fundamental nature, they are termed "obstacles to the ultimate and the conventional"; in reality, however, they are the obstacle of the active manifestation of coarse marks. When these marks of defilement and purity are viewed in relation to the marks of arising and ceasing, defilement and purity constitute the coarse.

Because it arises from the manifestation of cognitive obscurations (jñeyāvaraṇa) that grasp at these coarse characteristics, it is called the "obscuration of the manifestation of coarse characteristics.
It is about to be eliminated in the fifth stage, and one enters the sixth stage through the right abandonments (samyakprahāṇa).

Alternatively, based on the perspective of skillful means: by entering the fifth stage, one eliminates the obstacle of the mutual contradiction between the ultimate and the conventional; because one is then able to integrate the contemplation of these two, one enters the sixth stage. Since the preceding and succeeding stages mutually reflect one another, this is explained separately.
Sūtra: "In this stage, one eliminates the obstacles of the manifestation of views and enters the seventh stage.
Commentary: The "obstacles of the manifestation of views" refers to the obstacle of the active manifestation of subtle marks, which consists of clinging to the marks of arising and ceasing.

By means of the contemplation of dependent origination within the six stages, although the marks of defilement and purity are eliminated, one still perceives the marks of arising and ceasing; this obstructs the path of signlessness, whereby one does not see arising and ceasing. On the sublime path of signlessness, one indeed does not see arising and ceasing.
Now, this very mode of viewing is itself an obstruction, which is eliminated upon entering the seventh stage (*bhūmi*).

Alternatively, within the sixth stage, one practices the contemplation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), whereby one perceives the flow of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) but does not perceive the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Now, within the seventh stage, these two signs are eliminated because one is able to practice the contemplation of signlessness for a long duration.
Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Those who cling to the existence of arising still grasp at the subtle signs of arising within the process of saṃsāra."
"Those who cling to the existence of cessation still grasp at the subtle marks of returning to cessation and extinction.

The *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya Sūtra* and other texts likewise state: "There is no ignorance, and there is no exhaustion of ignorance. Exhaustion is precisely cessation; cessation is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Not perceiving the marks of cessation is the wondrous path of signlessness (*animitta-mārga*).
Raising the point that cessation is not perceived and arising is not perceived is called the "obstruction of the manifestation of subtle characteristics.
Compared to the coarse characteristics preceding form, this is termed the "obstruction of the manifestation of subtle views"; this is stated based on what is grasped as an object.
The mode of activity (*ākāra*) is precisely the mode of activity of arising and ceasing; it is the obstacle to seeing the mode of activity.
The Sūtra states: “In this stage, by removing the obstacle of not seeing the characteristic of cessation, one enters the eighth stage.”
The commentary states: The characteristic of cessation is itself the absence of characteristics (*animitta*).

Because one predominantly grasps the characteristic of cessation during the seventh stage and diligently seeks it through exclusive mental attention (*manasikāra*) on the signless, one is unable to spontaneously give rise to superior practices within emptiness; this constitutes an obstruction to the effortless, sublime contemplation of the signless (*anābhoga-animitta-vipaśyanā*).
Not perceiving the characteristic of cessation is the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta*).

Upon entering the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), one not only does not perceive the characteristic of cessation, but also does not perceive the two characteristics of signs and lands; therefore, one attains mastery over these two as well.
Therefore, within the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), two kinds of delusion are abandoned:
first, the delusion of exerting effort regarding the signless (*animitta*); second, the delusion of lacking mastery over signs.
For now, I shall mention only the former, as the latter is implicitly excluded by its presence.
Sūtra: "In this stage, having eliminated the obstacle of not seeing the characteristic of arising, one enters the ninth stage.
Commentary: Regarding "not seeing the characteristic of arising," in contrast to the aforementioned characteristic of cessation, this must refer to the characteristic of arising of all phenomena.

Because one enters the eighth stage and contemplates quiescence with joy, one does not perceive the characteristics of dependent origination; this is stated in terms of its general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

Nevertheless, in the eighth stage, one still lacks the desire to engage in the benefit of others, as one does not specifically perceive the existence of sentient beings and thus relinquishes the practice of benefiting them.
The *Treatise on the Eighth Ground* states: "Only after being exhorted seven times by the Buddhas does one emerge [from this stage], because of the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta*).
The eighth ground is able to subdue this obstacle of not perceiving sentient beings, thereby enabling entry into the ninth ground."
Another explanation is as follows:

Because one does not perceive sentient beings as being distinct from the body—since that which is born is oneself—one does not perceive sentient beings as existing separately outside the body; for this reason, one is able to constantly benefit them.

Now, because at the beginning of the eighth stage one perceives that there are distinct sentient beings outside of one's own body, this perception obstructs the non-perception of the characteristic of sentient beings; therefore, it is called an "obstruction.
Specifically, the obstruction consisting in not seeing sentient beings is termed the "obstruction of not seeing sentient beings."
Therefore, the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya* states: "In order to constantly benefit sentient beings, one contemplates ultimate emptiness.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* also says: "The ninth [hindrance] is the obstacle of being unwilling to act for the sake of others; therefore, upon entering the ninth stage, it can be completely severed."
Sūtra: "In this stage, one removes the obstacles to the six supernormal powers and enters the tenth stage.
Commentary: This refers to the obstacle consisting of a lack of mastery over all phenomena.
Mastery over phenomena refers to the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and the great wisdom of the Dharma.
Because of these obscurations, mastery is obstructed.
To provide an illustration, the six supernormal powers are cited here as representative of the great cloud of Dharma-wisdom.
Another explanation:
"Regarding all points of training (*śikṣāpada*), one is free from disrespect and calms the mind of agitation and regret" refers to the previously mentioned cultivation of causes.
"Entering the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*)" clarifies the fruit that is attained.

Subsequently, through the stage of the roots of goodness, because one has abandoned disrespect for the Triple Gem and the True Dharma, the obstacle of indolence is removed and all sins are extinguished.
Furthermore, by being able to abandon the obstacle of self-will, the mind’s agitation and regret are stilled.

As Vasubandhu’s *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "To practice within the internal mind while clinging to a self as a bodhisattva constitutes an obstruction to the mind and violates the path of non-abiding."
"One who does not abide in the path" refers to one in the first bhūmi who clings to the notion of "I" being able to practice, thereby contradicting the path of the first bhūmi.

As the Bodhisattva Asaṅga states in his *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: "To remove the obstacle of agitation caused by joy means that because one thinks, 'I am able to practice this sublime conduct,' much joy and agitation arise."
Joyful agitation is *auddhatya* (restlessness); taking this as an obstacle, it obstructs entry into the first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*).
By removing this obstacle, one gains entry into the first stage, which is to say that one becomes free from disrespect and so forth.
All of these belong to the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrva*), and do not constitute entry into the first ground (*prathamā bhūmi*).
The ten obstacles described below should be understood accordingly.

Because one practices the three kinds of giving (*tri-dāna*) within the first ground, one is able to benefit sentient beings; thus, by eliminating the obstructing factors that are contrary to this, one attains entry into the second ground.
In the second stage (*bhūmi*), one maintains ethical discipline; having removed the obstacle of afflicting sentient beings, one enters the third stage.
In the third stage, one cultivates meditative concentration (*samādhi*), removing the obstacle to the pliancy and purity of mind.

"Mind" refers here to the training of the mind; by removing all obstacles to concentration and departing from a rigid and forceful mind, it is called "pliancy and purity of mind," through which one enters the fourth stage.
Entering the fourth stage (*bhūmi*), one cultivates the contemplation of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*); this is called "skillful means.
Having eliminated these obstacles, one attains entry into the fifth stage.

Upon entering the fifth stage, one is able to cause the ultimate (*paramārtha*) and the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) to accord with one another without contradiction; therefore, by eliminating the obstacle of viewing the ultimate and the conventional as distinct, one attains entry into the sixth stage.

Entering the sixth stage, one practices the contemplation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), thereby removing the obstacles of perceiving the aspects of defilement and purity within the Four Noble Truths, and attains entry into the seventh stage.

Upon entering the seventh stage, one frequently practices the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta*), thereby removing the obstacles of perceiving the signs of arising and ceasing within dependent origination, and attains entry into the eighth stage.

Upon entering the eighth stage, one is able to spontaneously contemplate the principle of signlessness, eliminating the signs of increase and decrease; when pure dharmas arise, true suchness does not increase, and when afflictions are extinguished, true suchness does not decrease.
"Arising" means increasing; by mentioning what does not increase, that which does not decrease is implicitly revealed, whereby one enters the ninth stage (*navamī bhūmi*).
Upon entering the ninth stage, one should speak of the obstacle to the desire to act for the benefit of sentient beings;

however, speaking from the perspective of the stage of fulfillment, it is able to suppress and eliminate the obstacles to the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*). One should say that upon entering the tenth stage, one is able to eliminate the obstacles to the six supernormal powers, because the eleventh obstacle is eliminated at the stage of fulfillment of the tenth stage. Therefore, it is said that the ten stages eliminate the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), while the obstacle of the ninth stage is concealed and thus not discussed.
This interpretation accords with the literal text, while the former interpretation accords with the underlying principle;
yet, when also consulting the older translations, the latter interpretation is superior. Why is this so?
The old sūtras state in every instance that one "enters" after having "abandoned," making it clear that this does not refer to mere suppression (*vibhava*).
Alternatively, it may be that when suppression is complete, it is termed "having abandoned.
One may choose between these two interpretations according to one's own preference.
Sūtra: “In this stage, having eliminated the cognitive obstructions and having removed the fundamental mind, one enters the Tathāgata stage.
Commentary: The following clarifies the stage of fruition.
The first part clarifies the removal of hindrances to attain the perfection of the Buddha-ground; the latter reveals that the Buddha-ground possesses the three purities.

This is the former. Regarding the removal of the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*): the path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*) severs the subtle seeds and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the two hindrances. Since these preeminently obstruct enlightenment, it is said that one removes the cognitive hindrance. To "remove the fundamental mind" refers to the basis upon which the seeds and habitual tendencies rely.
The seventh type, which is free from defilement, is excluded because it is always associated with defilement.

The uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) abandons the remaining seven types of contaminated wholesome states, as well as the neutral states and their associated mental factors; these are termed the fundamental mind.

The eighth [consciousness] relies on both types of supports; the six consciousnesses rely solely on the support of habituation (*vāsanā*). Regarding the abandonment of this [eighth consciousness], there are two theories, as clarified in the tenth chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Sūtra: "The stage of the Tathāgata is called 'extremely pure' because it is purified by means of the three purities."
"What are the three?
First, the purification of afflictions; second, the purification of suffering; and third, the purification of characteristics.
The commentary states:
This reveals the threefold purity.
The textual section is divided into three parts: the heading, the inquiry, and the enumeration.
Purity from afflictions refers to the two obstacles and karma; purity from suffering refers to the two types of death; and purity of characteristics refers to habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Because of these three purities, there is nothing superior; it is called "ultimate purity.
As the Sūtra says: "For example, when true gold is melted, refined, and smelted, and has already been heated and beaten, it is free from all dust and impurities."
The commentary states: This is explained through metaphors.

There are four metaphors; the first three illustrate that the *dharmatā* and the *dharmakāya* are primordially pure, while the final one illustrates that the manifestation of *tathatājñāna* (the wisdom of suchness) is purified at the outset.
The dharmakāya is fundamentally pure in three ways, which correspond to the aforementioned three purities; the three metaphors follow this sequence.

However, the first two metaphors are combined with a single dharma, because the two causes—afflictions and karma—and their two effects follow one another, and thus they are combined under a single dharma.
Furthermore, the "three purities" refer to the three meanings of Dharmakāya, Prajñā, and Vimukti.

The Dharmakāya is fundamentally eternal like gold; Prajñā reflects and illuminates like water; and Vimukti is unimpeded like space. All are attained based on their inherent nature, as explained according to the principle of "one suchness."
The first section on analogies is divided into two parts: the first analogy illustrates present purity, while the latter establishes original existence.
This is the former.
For example, pure gold serves as an analogy for the state prior to the Path.
The process of melting, smelting, refining, and treating is a metaphor for the path;
once it has been burned, it is a metaphor for that which follows the path.
As the Sūtra states: "This is to reveal that the nature of gold is fundamentally pure."
"The golden substance is pure; it does not mean that there is no gold.
The commentary states: This analogy establishes that [the nature] is inherently present.
Regarding such passages, some scholars of the past have stated that the three bodies manifest as permanent, or that they are inherently permanent.
This is because through smelting, refining, and tempering, the original purity of the nature of gold is revealed.

The practice of the six perfections serves as the cause for the realization of the Dharma; because it removes defilements, one attains the purity of the golden essence, which does not mean that the gold itself is non-existent.
As the Sūtra says: "For example, when turbid water settles and becomes clear and pure, there is no longer any sediment."
The commentary states:
The divisions are as before, and their meaning may be understood by analogy.
The Sūtra says: "This is for the purpose of manifesting that the nature of water is fundamentally pure; it does not mean that there is no water."
The commentary states:

This serves as an analogy for the inherent existence [of the Buddha-nature]. The Sūtra says: "In this way, the Dharmakāya is intermingled with afflictions; once suffering and its origin have been eliminated, no residual habits remain. This is to manifest that the Buddha-nature is inherently pure; it does not mean that it lacks a substantial essence."
The Commentary states: This should be understood by means of an analogy.

The Sūtra says: "For example, as when the sky is obscured by smoke, clouds, dust, and mist, once these have been cleared away, the realm of space is pure; it is not that space itself has ceased to exist."
The commentary states:
"Similarity to emptiness" occurs prior to the path;
if it is eliminated, it occurs within the path.
Having already excluded the element of space (*ākāśadhātu*), following the path of purification, this is similar to the analogy taught in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*. The sūtra states:
"In this way, because all sufferings have been entirely exhausted, the dharmakāya is said to be pure; it does not mean that it lacks substance."
The commentary states:
The principle is consistent with the Dharma, and the textual characteristics are evident.
Sūtra: "For example, suppose there is a person who, while dreaming, sees a great river sweeping over and carrying away his body."
The commentary states:

The preceding analogy refers to the *dharmatā-tathatā* (the suchness of phenomena). When it is within the bonds of defilement (*saṃkleśa*), it is called the *tathāgatagarbha*; when it has emerged from those bonds, it is called the *dharmakāya*.
This also reveals that the nature of *nirvāṇa* is fundamentally pure; its manifestation as purity upon reaching the fruition is what is termed "attained through realization."
This is revealed through realization by means of wisdom; next, it is explained that the nature of this wisdom also exists from the beginningless past.
While in the causal stage, it is termed the "non-empty Tathāgatagarbha.

Upon reaching the stage where defilements are exhausted, the four types of wisdom-minds of Great Bodhi are what are attained as produced; these refer to their manifestation rather than the initial arising of seeds, for the seeds are inherently present from the start.
Therefore, the subsequent passage states: "This awakening is pure; it does not mean that there is no awakening.
This is as the *Śīla-sūtra* says: "The lineage of the spiritual family refers to the excellence of the six sense bases, which has been naturally acquired since beginningless time."

Regarding this mention of the "six sense bases," it is intended to mean that within the six sense bases, the mind base contains the seeds; this nature as a spiritual lineage (gotra) is beginningless and natural, being obtained by its very nature, and thus, through cultivation, one attains the great fruit.
The text is divided into three parts:
first, the analogy; second, the application; and third, the conclusion.
Within the analogy, there are five sections:

1. The analogy of the practitioner; 2. The analogy of currently abiding in ignorance; 3. The analogy of wearying of and fearing birth-and-death; 4. The analogy of aspiring for liberation through practice; 5. The analogy of realizing the falsity upon attaining the fruit.
In this regard, there are three [analogies]:
first, the analogy of a person who is able to practice;
second, the analogy of appearing to dwell in ignorance while in a dream.
Because ignorance is like the darkness of night or a dream, it is the cause of this cycle of birth and death; as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* quotes from a sutra: "Therefore, a sutra says:
'All classes of ordinary beings dwell perpetually in the long night, blinded by ignorance; their minds are shrouded in stupor and intoxication, never awakening.'"
Seeing his own body being swept away by the great river, he views it as an analogy for the terrors of birth and death.
Seeing its bitter fruit as being swept away like the river, it is either likened to being carried by the four flows through the five destinies.
"Seeing" refers to perception, which gives rise to weariness and fear.
The Sūtra says: "Moving hands and feet, one cuts across the stream and reaches the other shore.
The commentary states:
The analogy of aspiring for deliverance through practice:
moving the hands symbolizes cultivating sublime conduct;
moving the feet symbolizes abandoning the three obstacles.
The non-continuation of birth and death is likened to cutting off a stream.
When the stage of the Vajra is fulfilled, one speaks of having "crossed over.

While on the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), Bodhi remains in the future; because the causes are perfected and one is able to reach it, it is said that one has "attained the further shore" (*pāramitā*).
Sūtra: "Because his body and mind do not slacken or regress, once he has awakened from the dream, he no longer perceives the water or the distinction between this shore and the other.
Commentary: This is a metaphor for attaining the fruit and realizing that [the world] is illusory.
"By means of" refers to the causal basis; it refers to the diligent cultivation of the three types of karma throughout three great kalpas.
By citing both body and mind, one implicitly reveals the karma of speech.
Through unremitting and diligent practice, one ultimately attains Buddhahood.
"Fixed" means determined.
It is determined because of diligence that never slackens or regresses.

Having awakened from the dream, one stands upon the path of liberation; one sees neither this shore of the waters of birth and death, nor that shore of the fruit of nirvāṇa, because suchness and the wisdom of suchness are both without dual characteristics and are equal.
The "other shore" (pāra) consists of five aspects:
first, the object; second, the teaching; third, the principle; fourth, the practice; and fifth, the fruit.
To fully master these five is called "reaching the other shore" (pāramitā).

Sūtra: "It is not that there is no mind. Once the deluded thoughts of birth and death have been completely extinguished, this awakening is pure; it is not that there is no awakening. Commentary: It is said that this is not a state of non-mind. When the false conceptualizations of saṃsāra have been utterly exhausted, this is the purity of awakening; it does not mean that there is an absence of awakening.
This accords with the Dharma.
It merely accords with the general meaning; it is not necessarily a word-for-word correspondence.

This does not mean that the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) was originally non-existent, but rather that it is obstructed from arising by the heavy veils of deluded thought and ignorance (*avidyā*).
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Cheng weishi lun), fascicle five, cites a sutra stating: "The mind of true meaning is about to arise, yet it is constantly able to act as an obstacle," and so forth.

Through diligent cultivation of the three trainings, once delusive thoughts have been extinguished, one reaches the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*), which is the purity of awakening; this does not mean that the self-nature (*svabhāva*) is originally devoid of awakening.
The former statement, "it does not mean the absence of mind," refers to the meaning of the accumulation of mind, a term that applies to both cause and effect.
The latter statement, "it does not mean the absence of awareness," refers to the meaning of cognizing through awareness, a designation applied solely to the fruit.
Each [explanation] relies on a single meaning.
The Sūtra states: "Because all such false conceptualizations within the dharma-realm no longer arise, it is called 'pure'; it does not mean that the Buddhas lack actual substance."
The commentary states:
This is the "bond.

Such is the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); since the dharma-realm encompasses both principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*), the *Ratnagotravibhāga* explains the "element from beginningless time" (*anādikāliko dhātuḥ*) of the *Abhidharmasūtra* by relying on the perspective of suchness (*tathatā*).

The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* speak of the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) as the "beginningless element" (*anādikāliko dhātuḥ*); the *Ratnagotravibhāga* explains it based on its being the basis for both delusion and awakening, while the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and other texts explain it based on its being the basis for transmigration (*pravṛttyāśraya*). Since each relies on a single specific meaning, the term "dharma-dhātu" applies to both types.
Now, since this explanation of the *dhātus* concludes with the fourth [verse], it refers exclusively to the eighth *dhātu*, which is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and untainted (*anāsrava*).
If it were to comprehensively conclude all four [verses], it would encompass both principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*).
In this state, all tainted conceptualizations (*vikalpa*) do not arise, and the simultaneous arising of the four wisdoms is termed "purity."
It is not that the Buddhas originally lack this reality; rather, the untainted essence (*anāsrava-dhātu*) is termed "real" in contrast to the tainted (*sāsrava*).
The Sūtra states: "Furthermore, son of good family, this Dharma-body, being purified of the obstacles of affliction (*kleśāvaraṇa*), is able to manifest the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*)."
"When the karmic obstructions are purified, one can manifest the nirmāṇakāya;
when the cognitive obstructions are purified, one can manifest the dharmakāya.
The commentary states:
The fourth major section concludes the preceding discussion of cause and effect, announcing it so that it may be known.
It is further divided into three parts:

first, restating the preceding cause and effect to exhort belief and understanding; second, from "Good son, for this reason" onwards, providing a further extensive explanation; and third, from "Therefore, all Buddhas" onwards, establishing its supreme excellence.
This is the first [section].
Within it, there are further two parts:
first, restating cause and effect; second, exhorting one to believe and understand.
The first section further contains three parts:
first, the section on delineating the essence, which is the attainment of the body through the removal of hindrances;
second, the section on the mutual dependence of the body for its arising.
The subsequent passage restates the principle that based on causes one attains results.
Within the attainment of results, there is first the attainment of the result itself, followed by its non-differentiation [from the cause].
This constitutes the section on the exposition of the essential nature (*svabhāva*).
First, there is a general indication: the body accomplished through all dharmas of merit is collectively termed the *dharmakāya*.

Next, the following section specifically clarifies the attainment of the body through the severing of hindrances; that is, the *dharmakāya* fully endowed with the severance of hindrances such as the afflictions (*kleśa*).
That which causes the mind to lack decisiveness is called delusion (*moha*); the essence of delusion is itself an obstruction.
The fruits produced by both the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) and the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) constitute the essence of the afflictive obstruction (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
"Karma" refers to volitional construction; it refers to the three types of contaminated karma (*sāsrava-karman*), the very essence of which constitutes an obstruction.
"Wisdom" refers to the two types of uncontaminated wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*):

the fundamental and the subsequent. The essence of wisdom is not itself an obstruction; rather, because that which is to be known acts as an impediment such that wisdom does not arise, it is termed an "obstruction to wisdom. Thus, "obstruction to wisdom" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is named after the wisdom that is obstructed.

If it is called the "obstruction to the knowable" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), the knowable itself is not the obstruction; rather, because it covers the objects of knowledge and hinders the arising of wisdom, it is termed the "obstruction to the knowable.
Through the purification of the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), wisdom arises as the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*);
through the purification of the karmic obstructions (*karmāvaraṇa*), mastery over supernormal powers is attained as the Emanation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Through the purification of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), the reality that was previously shrouded becomes manifest as the *dharmakāya*.
As the Sūtra states: "For example, lightning flashes from space, and light emanates from the lightning."

"In this way, by relying on the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), one is able to manifest the Enjoyment-body (saṃbhogakāya); by relying on the Enjoyment-body, one is able to manifest the Transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya).
Commentary: This cites the section on arising in reliance [on the bodies], with the first being the analogy and the latter being the application of the principle.
The essence of emptiness is pervasive and eternal, and its nature is fundamentally pure; therefore, it is likened to the Dharma-body.
Its manifestations and transformations are impermanent; therefore, they are likened to flashes of lightning.
This can be understood through their respective origins.

Sūtra: “Because of the purity of its nature, it can manifest the Dharma-body; because wisdom is pure, it can manifest the Response-body; because samādhi is pure, it can manifest the Transformation-body.”
The commentary states:
This is the section on attaining the fruit based on the cited causes;
this is the attainment of the fruit.
Sūtra: “These three purities are the suchness of phenomena, the non-differentiated suchness, the single-flavored suchness, the liberated suchness, and the ultimate suchness.”
The commentary states:

Although there are three numbers within the section on attaining the fruit, there are no three distinct entities. The first [section] subsumes function back into nature, and the second concludes that they are not different.
This is the first.
These three purities do not depart from suchness; therefore, they are the suchness of dharmas.
Since the essence of suchness is not distinct, it does not differ from suchness.
Because it is uniquely untainted, it is the single flavor of suchness.
Because it is free from bondage, it is the suchness of liberation;
because it realizes the fulfillment of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), it is ultimate suchness.
As the Sūtra says: "Therefore, the essence of all Buddhas is without difference."
The commentary states:
"The bonds are not different.
Because the five preceding [realities] are suchness (tathatā), the essence of all Buddhas is not different."
This indicates that by practicing accordingly, all shall attain [this realization]; therefore, it is said that the essence of all Buddhas is without difference. Sūtra: “Good son!

If there are good sons or good daughters who declare that the Tathāgata is their Great Teacher, and if they form such a resolute faith, these persons should, with a profound mind, understand that the body of the Tathāgata is without distinction.”
The commentary states:
This is an exhortation to inspire faith and understanding.
The purpose of inspiring faith and understanding is to serve as the skillful means for cultivation.
It says, "O son of good family," addressing the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha.

From the words "If there be" onwards, it means that any man or woman who can simply say, "The Buddha is my teacher," and possesses resolute faith, such a person will be able to deeply understand and realize that the Tathāgata is without distinction [from all Buddhas].
Some say that one who regards the Tathāgata as their great teacher and can develop resolute faith should understand him with a profound mind (*gambhīra-citta*) exactly as he has taught.

Others exhort those prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) to develop resolute faith in the non-differentiation of the Tathāgata, while Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*) should understand the Tathāgata with a profound mind as being without distinction.

Sūtra: “Good son! For this reason, one completely eliminates all improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) toward all objects of experience; one then knows that those phenomena possess no dual characteristics and are free from the conceptual distinctions practiced by the noble ones.”
The commentary states:
The subsequent section further elaborates on this in two parts:

first, a detailed explanation that the cause and effect are no different from those previously mentioned; second, beginning with "One who sees thus," a detailed explanation of the preceding faith and understanding.

This first section is divided into five parts: first, the arising of superior practice regarding the object; second, the inability to sever hindrances despite suchness; third, the perfection of the cause, from "Suchness is all... onwards; fourth, the fulfillment of the fruit, from "Suchness is the dharma-realm... onwards; and fifth, the conclusion that there is no difference, from "All hindrances... onwards.
This is the first [point].
For this reason, it is the term used to introduce [the subject]:
regarding all objects, that is, the objects of knowledge.
Because one does not engage in correct reflection (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) regarding this object, one perceives divergent characteristics and is unable to practice;

when one can engage in correct reflection, one realizes that there is no duality of objects and no false discrimination, and since wisdom is free from dualistic marks, one is able to initiate practice—this is the practice cultivated by the noble ones (*ārya*).
Sūtra: “Because one correctly practices suchness by means of the absence of dualistic characteristics therein, in this way and thus all obstacles are completely eliminated.

Commentary: It is said that one can sever obstacles and can perceive the absence of dualistic characteristics in each respective [object], hence it says, “suchness by means of the absence of dualistic characteristics therein.”
Since the obstacles to be abandoned are numerous and arise in a continuous succession, one must repeatedly address them as they occur.
Thus, the Sūtra states: "To the extent that all obstacles are extinguished, to that same extent, the *dharmatathatā* and the *tathatājñāna* attain supreme purity."
The commentary states:
The perfection of the cause is attained at the stage of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the Vajra-like Samādhi.
To enumerate the extinction of the ten obstacles, it says: "As suchness, all obstacles are extinguished."
Regarding the distinctions between the suchness realized and the wisdom attained across the ten stages, it is further stated: "The dharma-realm of suchness and correct wisdom are pure;

in this way and that way, all sovereign powers are fully embraced and brought to accomplishment. *Sūtra* passage: "The dharma-realm of suchness and correct wisdom are pure; in this way and that way, all sovereign powers are fully embraced and brought to accomplishment."
The commentary states:
The fulfillment of the attainment of the fruit occurs within the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

All sovereign powers are the three bodies (*trikāya*), and all meritorious qualities are not separate from the three bodies; therefore, it is said that by fully embracing them, all are brought to accomplishment.
Sūtra: “Because all obstacles are entirely eliminated and all obstacles are rendered pure, this is called the true characteristic of suchness and correct wisdom.”
The commentary states:
There is no difference in their nature as fetters.
Because all obscurations are extinguished and all obscurations are purified, one realizes the suchness of purity.
This very purity is called the true characteristic of suchness and correct wisdom.
This true characteristic is the characteristic of non-duality.
As the Sūtra says: “One who sees in this way is said to have the noble vision; this is what is called truly seeing the Buddha.”
Why is this? Because they have perceived the true suchness (*tathatā*) of phenomena as it truly is. Commentary:
This expands upon the preceding section on faith and understanding (*adhimukti*). It is divided into three parts:

first, causing [the practitioner] to know as if they had realized it themselves; second, from "Therefore, all Buddhas... onwards, clarifying that they are identical to all Buddhas; and third, from "However, all Tathāgatas... onwards, concluding with the realization of reality (*tattva-darśana*).
This is the first [section].
First, it is presented as it was realized; second, the reason for this is investigated; and finally, it is formally explained.
"Noble" (*ārya*) means correct, and "vision" (*darśana*) means understanding.
To know [the Buddha] exactly as it has been realized is right understanding (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*).
Alternatively, because an ordinary person can, through faith and understanding, accord with the realization-vision of the noble ones, they truly see the Buddha.
The explanation of this inquiry may be understood from the scripture: "Therefore, all Buddhas are able to see all Tathāgatas universally.
The commentary states:
This clarifies that [the Buddha] is equal to all Buddhas.
The text is divided into three parts:
first, the Buddha’s universal knowledge; second, the failure of the two vehicles to understand; and third, the inability of ordinary beings to fathom it.
This is the first [point].
Because one perceives that the principle of suchness (tathatā) is perfect and non-dual, one perceives all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
Sūtra: "For what reason?"
"Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have already transcended the three realms, yet they are unable to know or see the true reality.
The commentary states:
"The two vehicles do not realize it."
First the inquiry, then the explanation. Why is this?
Only the Buddha knows all things universally.

Although noble beings of the two vehicles with fixed dispositions have transcended the three realms, because they lack the seed of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), even if they seek the true reality, they cannot know it with their fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) nor perceive it with their subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*); or rather, they cannot know it through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) nor perceive it through inference (*anumāna*).

Sūtra: “Thus, that which the noble ones do not know or see causes all ordinary people to give rise to doubt and confusion; through their inverted conceptualizations, they are unable to attain liberation.”
The commentary states:
Ordinary beings cannot fathom this.
First is the principle (*dharma*), next is the analogy (*upamāna*), and finally is the application (*upanaya*).
This is the Dharma.
Foolish people lacking the [spiritual] lineage cannot fathom it; they either doubt its non-existence or, through inverted attachment, falsely conceive of it as a self.
As the Sūtra says: "It is like a rabbit attempting to swim across the ocean—it can certainly not get through."
"Why is this? Because their power is feeble and inferior. Zan said:
This is an analogy.
First is the heading, second is the inquiry, and third is the explanation.
Because there is no noble lineage and only outflows (*āsrava*), and because the power of their wisdom is weak and inferior, they are unable to cross over.
The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states: "I do not reveal this to the foolish and the ignorant, fearing that they would conceptualize it and grasp it as a self.
The Bodhisattva Dharmapāla and others explain: "Foolish" (*bāla*) refers to those who lack the [Mahāyāna] nature, and "ignorant" (*mūḍha*) refers to those who seek only their own peace.

Furthermore, this may refer to ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles at a stage when their faculties are not yet matured and thus cannot comprehend it, whereas those with matured faculties can know it.
Alternatively, as stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the three vehicles do not know it; this is based on their knowledge being incomplete.
Only the Buddha possesses perfect knowledge;
to say that he does not know is to attempt to interpret his words according to your own capacity, which is truly extraordinary.
As the Sūtra says: "Ordinary people are also like this, for they cannot penetrate the suchness of phenomena."
The commentary states: This is consistent with the Dharma.
Because there is no fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), one cannot penetrate; because there is no subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*), one cannot reach [the goal].

Sūtra: "However, all Tathāgatas possess a non-conceptual mind; because they have attained great mastery over all phenomena and are endowed with pure, profound wisdom, this is their own domain, not shared with others."
The commentary states:
This concludes the realization of the truth.

Because the Buddha is free from conceptual discrimination and does not perceive dualistic characteristics, he realizes the suchness (*tathatā*) of phenomena and penetrates the true mark of emptiness of all dharmas; thus, he attains great mastery over all phenomena.
Because one attains wisdom that accords with suchness (*tathatā*), one is fully endowed with profound wisdom.
For this reason, it is exclusively the domain of the Buddha and is not shared by others.
As the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata says that prajñāpāramitā is indeed not prajñāpāramitā; it is called 'pāramitā' [only as a designation]."
The Bodhisattva Devaśrī’s commentary states:
“When speaking of the *pāramitās*, they belong exclusively to the Buddha’s ‘other shore.
That which is not a *pāramitā* is not the ‘other shore’ for any other person.”
That which is called a *pāramitā* is the binding of this Buddha’s other shore.
This is also like that. The Sūtra says:

“Therefore, throughout immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, did not spare their own bodies or lives and performed difficult practices and ascetic austerities, before finally attaining this body which is supreme and peerless, inconceivable, beyond the realm of verbal expression, wondrously tranquil, and free from all fears.”
The commentary states:
This concludes the section on the sublime excellence.
Regarding the immeasurable ascetic practices, these constitute the causal basis for such conduct.
Not sparing one's own body or life is due to four causes and conditions:
first, for the sake of seeking the Dharma, as in the case of the youth of the Snowy Mountains;
second, for the sake of repaying kindness, as in the case of Prince Dharmapāla and others.
Third is to rescue the poor, as in the case of the Golden Lion and others;
fourth is to save lives, as in the case of Prince Sattva and others.
Only by doing so can one obtain this body and manifest the attainment of the fruit.
"Supreme, peerless, and so forth" is a praise of the excellent fruit.

It is "unsurpassed" because it is ultimate; "peerless" because it has no equal; "inconceivable" because it transcends conceptual thought; "beyond verbal expression" because it exceeds the scope of linguistic description; "wondrously tranquil" because it is Great Nirvāṇa; and "free from the five fears" because birth-and-death have ceased—namely, the fear of lacking a livelihood, the fear of death, the fear of the miserable realms, the fear of ill repute, and the fear of assemblies.

Sūtra: “Good son! One who thus knows and sees the *tathatā* (suchness) of phenomena has no birth, aging, death, or limited lifespan; they have neither sleep nor hunger or thirst, and their mind is always in meditative concentration without distraction or movement.”
Commentary: The third major section below concludes with an exhortation to practice.
The text is divided into three parts:

First, the preceding section on faith and understanding is concluded by urging one to rely upon practice; second, from "However, all Tathāgatas... onwards, the preceding section on attaining the fruit is concluded by urging one to seek realization; third, from "If a good son... onwards, the two preceding meanings are established.
The beginning consists of three parts:
first, the presentation of the benefits of faith and understanding; second, the presentation of the harms of lack of faith; and third, the exposition of the benefits to encourage practice.
This is the first part.

If one can, for even a single moment, thus know and see the *tathatā* of phenomena, one shall attain *bodhi* forever free from birth, aging, death, and so forth; because this serves as a remote cause, one will certainly attain it.

Therefore, the "Bhaiṣajyarāja Chapter" of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "Those who hear this sūtra shall neither grow old nor die; before long, they will take grass and sit at the site of enlightenment."

If the virtues of the Tathāgata have already been fully explained previously and are stated again in the subsequent text, then this present statement refers to the fruit to be attained by those who possess faith and understanding (*śraddhādhimukta*).
Alternatively, it may be that the virtues of the Tathāgata are reiterated two or three times to inspire faith and understanding.

Because he has attained the vajra-body, he is free from birth, old age, and death; because he is detached from the five hindrances, he is free from sleep; because he has shattered the armies of Māra, he is free from hunger and thirst; the rest of the text may be understood accordingly.
Nevertheless, the previous explanation of the knots is excellent.
The Sūtra states: "If one gives rise to a mind of contention toward the Tathāgata, then one will be unable to see the Tathāgata. Commentary:
Lack of faith causes harm.

To give rise to a mind of contentious debate and be unable to believe and understand is precisely what prevents one from realizing the three bodies of the Tathāgata in the future, nor being able to perceive the Tathāgata through inference based on the teachings.
Sūtra: "All that is spoken by the Buddhas is able to benefit. Commentary:
This praises the benefits of the teaching and exhorts one to practice it.
First the thesis, then the explanation.
This is the thesis. Sūtra:

"Those who hear [this teaching] shall all attain liberation; they shall not encounter malevolent beasts, wicked people, or evil spirits. Because of hearing the Dharma, their karmic retribution shall be inexhaustible."
The commentary states:
This explains the benefits obtained.
First, one attains nirvāṇa; second, one is free from harm; and finally, the karmic retribution is inexhaustible.
The *Prajñā-śāstra* states: "With respect to the Dharma, it serves as the cause of realization (*vibhāva-hetu*) and also as the cause for subsequent birth.
That one attains liberation by listening to the sutras refers to the cause of realization.
Regarding "inexhaustible fruition," this refers to the attainment of *bodhi*, which is the cause of birth.

As stated in the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya*: "One who practices this Dharma attains an immeasurable mass of merit; because it is supreme and inexhaustible, it results from the non-cessation of benefiting others."
"Because the karmic fruit of hearing the Mahāyāna is superior, it transcends the two vehicles.
Because great compassion for the benefit of others is unceasing, it is inexhaustible.
By means of these, one shall never encounter any evils."
Sūtra: "However, all Tathāgatas have no records of things not known; regarding all objective realms, they have no desire to know them.
Commentary: This concludes the preceding section on attaining the fruit and exhorts one to seek realization.
This section is divided into two parts:
first, concluding the discussion on the results attained to inspire joy; second, clarifying the benefits gained from hearing [this teaching] to exhort others to practice and study.

Regarding the conclusion of the fruits attained, although there are infinite varieties, this text specifically concludes with the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) and the merits of great compassion for one's own benefit and the benefit of others, as these implicitly reveal the remainder.
First, the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) are summarized; subsequently, compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā*) is summarized.
Within the first section there are five points: first, regarding "no non-recording," there is nothing he does not clearly record, and there is no loss of mindfulness.
First, among the four modes of deportment, there is nothing not subsumed by wisdom, because wisdom precedes them all.
Second, regarding all objects of experience, there is no desire to know them [as separate], which means that aspiration does not diminish.
Alternatively, all objects are known spontaneously, without needing to seek them out before one can understand them.
As the Sūtra says: "There is no thought of difference between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa; whatever the Tathāgata has predicted is invariably certain."
The commentary states:
Third, there is no perception of diversity.
Fourth, because his knowledge of the three periods of time is free from obstruction, there is nothing among the teachings he proclaims that is not definitive.
Furthermore, because the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) can know the various dharma-gates such as the aggregates (*skandha*), what is taught is definitive.
Alternatively, it is because of the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), or because verbal action is preceded by wisdom (*jñānapūrvamgama*), that what is spoken is definitive.
Sūtra: “In the four modes of deportment of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, there is nothing that is not encompassed by wisdom. Commentary:
Fifth, because bodily action is preceded by wisdom, there is nothing that is not encompassed by wisdom.
Sūtra: “There is not a single phenomenon that is not encompassed by loving-kindness and compassion, nor is there any that does not bring benefit and peace to all sentient beings.
Commentary: This concludes the previously attained merit of great loving-kindness and great compassion for the sake of others.
To benefit others is to extract them from suffering; to grant peace is to bestow happiness.
Because of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), one extracts them from suffering to benefit them; because of great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), one bestows happiness and peace.

Furthermore, the Buddha’s fundamental vow was solely to benefit others; having cultivated great compassion and loving-kindness to seek the unsurpassed fruit, all his actions are without exception encompassed by compassion.

Furthermore, the "unshared" [qualities] are cited to show the excellence of self-benefit, while "compassion" is cited to show the excellence of benefiting others; thus, these two categories are briefly summarized. Sūtra: "Good son!..."
"If there are good sons or good daughters who hear, believe, and understand this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama Sūtra*...
[The commentary] states:
This clarifies the benefits gained from hearing [the teaching] and exhorts others to practice and study it.
The text is divided into four sections:
first, clarifying the benefits gained from hearing; second, the inquiry; third, the explanation; and fourth, the conclusion.
Regarding the first section, it begins with faith and understanding upon first hearing the sutra, followed by the clarification of the benefits gained.
Hearing refers to the wisdom of hearing; faith refers to the wisdom of reflection; and understanding refers to the wisdom of cultivation.
Alternatively, this may refer to the most inferior level, wherein one is able to believe and understand solely through the wisdom of hearing.
If even those who merely possess faith and understanding—not yet having attained realization—obtain such merit, how much more so for those of superior practice?

Sūtra: “They shall not fall into the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, or asuras; they shall always dwell among humans and devas, never being born into lowly or base conditions; they shall constantly have the opportunity to draw near to all Buddhas and Tathāgatas to hear and receive the True Dharma; and they shall always be reborn in the pure lands of the Buddhas.”
The commentary states:
Regarding the benefits received, one is freed from the eight difficulties.
First, being freed from the three evil realms constitutes three [difficulties].
Asuras, according to the Hīnayāna, are subsumed under the destinies of hungry ghosts and animals;
according to the Mahāyāna, they are subsumed under the destiny of devas, specifically within the category of peripheral regions (*pratyanta*).
Those born as humans or devas are the reverse of the aforementioned evil destinies and peripheral regions.
Not being born into lowly circumstances means that one eliminates birth with impaired faculties, such as being blind from birth or deaf from birth.
"Constantly attaining proximity to the Buddha" means being free from the difficulties of being before or behind the Buddha.
"Hearing the True Dharma" means being free from the difficulty of possessing worldly wisdom and eloquence.
One will always be born in a Buddha-land and be free from the hardships of the long-lived devas.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, the four wheels eliminate the eight difficulties (*aṣṭākṣaṇa*):

first, dwelling in a favorable place, namely a central land (*madhyadeśa*), which removes five difficulties, namely the three evil destinies, the long-lived heavens, and the difficulty of being in a border region.
Second, relying on virtuous persons, which means encountering a Buddha—excluding those born before or after a Buddha’s appearance.
Third, formulating right aspirations, which refers to right view—excluding wrong views and worldly cleverness.
Those who have planted roots of goodness over four lifetimes—excluding those with impaired faculties—now hear this sutra;
because they are able to believe and understand it while fully avoiding the eight difficulties, its power is superior, as it is capable of removing obstacles.
Not only does it eliminate obstacles, but one also swiftly attains bodhi; this is explained below in the section on "Distinguishing the Middle.
The Sūtra asks: "For what reason?
The Commentary says:
This is a sign of inquiry.
Why is it that upon hearing this sutra, one is able to believe and understand it, and is able to eliminate the causes of the eight difficulties?
The sutra says: "It is because one has been able to hear this most profound Dharma."
The commentary says:
This is an explanation.
By upholding the Mahāyāna, one accumulates ten merits:

First, the accomplishment of the seeds of all roots of goodness; second, the attainment of all joy and bliss at the time of death; third, the attainment of birth according to one's wishes in all places; fourth, the attainment of the wisdom of recollecting births by nature in all places of rebirth; fifth, always encountering the Buddhas in the places where one is born; sixth, constantly remaining in the presence of the Buddhas to hear the Mahāyāna Dharma; seventh, the accomplishment of the faculty of superior faith; eighth, the accomplishment of the faculty of superior wisdom; ninth, the attainment of being far removed from the two obstacles of afflictions and knowledge; and tenth, the swift accomplishment of unsurpassed bodhi.
For this reason, they remain far removed from the eight difficulties.
The Sūtra says: "These sons and daughters of good family have already been known and prophesied by the Tathāgata; they shall attain non-retrogression in their pursuit of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
The commentary states:
This establishes the preceding reason.

Those who are able to hear this sutra and give rise to faith and understanding have already been known by the Tathāgata through their mental bodies (*nāmakāya*) and have already been seen by him through their physical bodies (*rūpakāya*).
It is explained that the merits of this person are known and seen only by the Buddha, while others cannot know or see them.
If one says "know," why rely on the word "see"?
If one says "see," why need one say "know"?

Answer: According to Vasubandhu’s *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is said: "The Buddha does not know through the cognition of results; he perceives them directly through his vow-knowledge (*praṇidhijñāna*).
However, when it is simply said that he "knows," this refers to the Buddha seeing the result and inferring its cause; therefore, it is here stated that he "perceives" it.
The seer possesses the wisdom of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*) and can comprehend [the object] by raising the mind.
If this is so, why is it necessary to say "knows" when one simply "sees"?
It is because while one merely sees the form (*rūpa*), one is now also able to know the body consisting of the other four aggregates (*skandha*).
This is not something produced by effort, but is known and seen only by the Buddha; thus, it is remembered by the Buddha.
Furthermore, one shall attain non-retrogression from bodhi.
Although it is not attained immediately, one shall be able to realize it.

In whichever stage one may be, one shall realize the four types of non-retrogression—namely, the four kinds of non-retrogression consisting of faith (*śraddhā*), abiding (*vihāra*), realization (*sākṣātkriyā*), and practice (*caryā*): non-retrogression of faith occurs at the sixth mind of the ten stages of faith;
non-retrogression of abiding occurs at the seventh mind of the ten stages of abiding;
and non-retrogression of realization occurs at the first bhūmi.
Non-retrogression in practice occurs upon entering the eighth stage.

As the Sūtra states: "If a son of good family or a daughter of good family hears this profound and subtle Dharma but once, it should be known that such a person does not slander the Tathāgata, does not disparage the True Dharma, and does not slight the Noble Assembly."
The commentary states:
To further elaborate upon the two aforementioned superior benefits and to encourage the hearing, acceptance, and practice of this sutra,
there are three superior benefits:
First, not slandering the Triple Gem; second, increasing roots of goodness; third, causing the practice of the six perfections.
This is the first [of these].
Because one knows that the Buddha is eternally abiding, one does not slander the Tathāgata by saying that he has entered ultimate extinction.
Because one knows that the teaching is definitive, one does not slander the Dharma.
Because one knows that [enlightenment] can be attained, one does not slander the Saṅgha.
Furthermore, because hearing and faith serve as the causes for indestructible faith, one does not slander, destroy, or treat with contempt the Triple Gem.

Sūtra: “In order that all sentient beings who have not yet planted roots of goodness may plant them, and those who have already planted roots of goodness may cause them to increase and reach maturity.
Commentary: This refers to the increasing of roots of goodness.
This causes those who have not yet resolved to seek awakening to resolve to seek it, thereby planting roots of merit.

For those who have already resolved to seek it, it causes [those roots] to increase; during the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*), it causes them to progress through the first *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*, to extend through the second *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*, and to bring them to fulfillment in the third *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*.

However, regarding the two aforementioned categories, it is merely stated that those who hear the sutras obtain the six pāramitās and cause others to practice them; this is a mutual illustration, meaning that both self and others are likewise so.
Sūtra: “Exhort all sentient beings in all worlds to practice the six pāramitās. Commentary:
This means that later [the bodhisattva] is able to cause them to practice the six perfections.
This passage clarifies that by hearing and believing for oneself, one can accomplish these three [virtues].
Having heard them, one subsequently transforms others through these three activities.
Furthermore, one is able to believe and understand, thereby destroying the four kinds of obstacles.
First, by not slandering the Buddha and so forth, one removes the obstacle of the icchantika’s lack of faith;
by causing them to plant roots of goodness, one removes the obstacle of non-Buddhists’ attachment to a self;
and by practicing all six perfections, one removes the śrāvaka’s fear of suffering and the pratyekabuddha’s mind of renunciation.
Since there are many benefits, one should practice the conduct that brings benefit to both oneself and others.

The Sūtra says: At that time, the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, along with Brahmā, Śakra, the Four Heavenly Kings, and the assembly of devas, rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, joined their palms in reverence, and prostrated at the feet of the Buddha.
The commentary states:
This fourth major section of the chapter concerns the reception of understanding, the upholding, and the practice.
The text is divided into four parts:

First, reverently receiving and understanding; second, from "World-Honored One, we... onwards, making vows to uphold and study; third, the World-Honored One’s praise and seal of approval; fourth, exhorting wide circulation.
Regarding the beginning and middle [of the discourse]: first there is reverent devotion, and subsequently there is understanding and realization. This refers to that reverent devotion.
Having heard the supreme Dharma, he manifests his advancement toward Bodhi; therefore, rising from his seat signifies that he shall become a Buddha.
Manifesting auspicious omens, he bared his right shoulder.

Because his mind accorded with the principles of the teachings, he joined his palms; because his heart was filled with reverence, he paid homage; and because his respect grew ever deeper, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.
The Sūtra states: He addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One!
In whatever place this subtle and wondrous *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* is expounded, that land shall enjoy four kinds of benefit.”
The commentary states:
This is the section on "Comprehension.
It consists of four parts:
First, the heading; second, the inquiry; third, the explanation; fourth, the conclusion.
This is the heading.
He addressed the Buddha to awaken him to that which is to be known.
Because he invokes the Honored Title, it is called "World-Honored One" (*Bhagavān*).
Because it points to what has been realized and understood, it says, "if one preaches such a scripture as the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*.
